items.title: Magna Carta was annulled within ten weeks
items.claim: King John sealed Magna Carta at Runnymede on 15 June 1215. What happened next?

options.text: It immediately became the basis of English liberty and was respected by the crown
John wrote to Pope Innocent III, who annulled it as 'shameful and demeaning' on 24 August 1215 — civil war resumed
John was forced to confirm it in Parliament the following year
It was burned by the barons after John refused to enforce it

items.reveal:
Pope Innocent III's bull of 24 August 1215 declared Magna Carta 'null and void of all validity forever', calling it extorted by force. The First Barons' War followed; the barons invited Prince Louis of France to take the throne.

John died of dysentery in October 1216. The charter was reissued by the regents of his nine-year-old son Henry III to win support — that is the version that took root. The 1297 reissue under Edward I is the one on the statute roll.
items.why: Magna Carta as 'the foundation of liberty' is a 17th-century invention (Coke). In 1215 it was a peace treaty between a desperate king and rebellious barons — and it failed within weeks.

items.title: Clause 39 of Magna Carta is the ancestor of due process
items.claim: What does Clause 39 of Magna Carta (1215) say?

options.text: 'No free man shall be seized or imprisoned, or stripped of his rights or possessions... except by the lawful judgment of his equals or by the law of the land' — the basis of habeas corpus and due process traditions

items.reveal:
The 1215 charter had 63 clauses, mostly about specific feudal grievances. Clause 39 (combined with clause 40 — 'to no one will we sell, to no one deny or delay right or justice') is the source of the due process tradition.

'Free man' (liber homo) in 1215 was a small minority — perhaps a tenth of the population. The protection was extended over centuries by reissue, interpretation and common-law development.

The US Fifth Amendment (1791) — 'nor be deprived of life, liberty, or property, without due process of law' — directly echoes Magna Carta. The phrase 'due process of law' was first used in a 1354 reissue of the charter under Edward III.
items.why: Founding documents have specific clauses that travel further than others. Clause 39 of Magna Carta is the single most influential sentence in English-language constitutional law — its 21st-century echoes are direct.

items.title: The Domesday Book recorded almost every pig in England
items.claim: William I commissioned the Domesday survey in 1085, completed 1086. How detailed was it?

options.text: It listed only the major landholders and royal manors
It recorded landholders, ploughs, mills, fishponds, livestock and even individual peasants down to the level of swineherds — over 13,000 places
It was a list of military obligations only

items.reveal_title: Not one ox or cow escaped
items.reveal:
The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (E text) complained: 'So very narrowly did he have it investigated that there was no single hide nor a yard of land, nor indeed (it is a shame to relate but it seemed no shame to him to do) one ox nor one cow nor one pig which was left out.'

Commissioners visited every shire, took sworn testimony, and produced the survey in around a year. The original manuscripts (Great Domesday and Little Domesday) survive at The National Archives, Kew.
items.why: Medieval government is often dismissed as primitive. Domesday is more administratively detailed than anything attempted in Europe for centuries afterwards.
